mode.name: Micro Case
mode.description: A compact before/after style mini case study.
mode.structure: Before (starting situation) -> what changed -> after (outcome) -> CTA.
mode.avoid: Use only outcomes supported by real proof; never fabricate metrics or results.

hook.instruction: Open by stating a popular myth you are about to break.
hook.exampleForm: "More cleaning product means cleaner. It does not."
hook.forbidGeneric: Do not open with "Let's talk about a common myth."

concept.title: Nine Weeks Ago
concept.core_idea: A micro case told entirely from a stranger's point of view. A potential customer Googles a local SaaS tool, finds their Instagram link in the bio, taps it — and lands on a feed where the last post is nine weeks old. The video walks through the exact mental checklist that stranger runs in the next thirty seconds, and the quiet decision they make before closing the app. The before is the feed as it exists. The change is the stranger's internal logic. The after is the business they choose instead.
concept.product_role: fenrik Studio is introduced at the resolution point as the practical fix — not a creative tool, not a platform, just a service that keeps the feed moving so the signal stays on. The proof point used is that the first content package is free and requires only a website URL, which removes the barrier that caused the silence in the first place.
concept.why_it_works: The Micro Case structure works here because the before and after are separated by nothing more than a stranger's thirty-second attention span — which makes the stakes feel immediate rather than abstract. The Reporter voice keeps it from feeling preachy. The POV shift to the potential customer is fresh against recent fingerprints, which stayed inside the founder's or team's perspective. The myth hook opens by stating that a quiet feed is just a cosmetic problem — then the case dismantles that assumption through observable customer behavior rather than opinion.
concept.narrative_arc: BEFORE: A stranger discovers a brand through a Google search result. Everything looks credible — clean website, decent reviews, professional bio. They tap the Instagram link. The feed loads. Last post: nine weeks ago. CHANGE: The video narrates the stranger's thought process in real time, framed as a series of brief, factual observations — 'Still operating? Hard to tell.' / 'Competitor has posted eleven times this month.' / 'Going with the other one.' No drama. No accusation. Just the logic. AFTER: The brand with the active feed gets the inquiry. The brand with the quiet one does not. The video closes with a single factual statement: a feed that stopped is a signal, whether the business meant to send it or not. Then the CTA frames fenrik Studio as the thing that keeps the signal on.
concept.emotional_tone: Quiet and unsettling — not alarming, just factual. The discomfort comes from recognition, not exaggeration. The stranger is not hostile; they are simply making a reasonable decision with the information available. That neutrality is what makes it land.
concept.audience_insight: Founders and small teams rarely think about what their inactive feed communicates to a stranger — they think about the content they haven't made yet, not the impression the silence is already making. Flipping to the customer's POV makes the cost of inactivity concrete without lecturing.

visual_direction.palette: Muted warm neutrals for the background and UI chrome — off-white, light sand, soft grey. The inactive feed thumbnails are slightly desaturated to visually reinforce staleness. One accent color (a clean teal or slate blue) used only for the annotation text to keep it readable.
visual_direction.lighting: Bright, ambient daylight — the kind of light that reads as a casual midday scroll, not a late-night crisis. Neutral and unhurried.
visual_direction.environment: No physical room or desk. The entire visual world is the phone screen — a simulated Instagram profile grid filling the frame, with a faint suggestion of a hand holding the phone at the bottom edge. Keeps the viewer inside the stranger's experience rather than observing it from outside.
visual_direction.camera_style: Static frame with subtle zoom-in on specific UI elements as the narration references them — the date stamp on the last post, the competitor's active grid visible in a side-by-side cut. No handheld movement. Cuts are deliberate and slow, matching the pace of someone scrolling and deciding.
visual_direction.art_direction: Screen-native aesthetic — the video is framed as if the viewer is watching someone else's phone screen in real time. Clean UI overlays simulate an Instagram profile page loading. Text annotations appear as brief, handwritten-style captions floating near relevant screen elements, mimicking the stranger's internal monologue. No talking head. No voiceover actor visible. The product never appears as a logo until the final frame.

package.title: Nine Weeks Ago
package.hook: Nine weeks of silence — what does that say about your business?
package.scenario: A solo SaaS founder checks their own Instagram profile while reviewing their website analytics and realizes the last post went up the day before a product launch — nine weeks ago. The website looks professional. The social feed looks abandoned. They had not considered that a potential customer would see both in the same session.

video.script:
[SCENE 1 — Phone screen fills frame. Instagram profile grid loads. Thumbnails slightly desaturated. Date stamp visible: '9 weeks ago.']
VO: Nine weeks of silence — what does that say about your business?

[SCENE 2 — Subtle zoom onto the profile bio and grid. Annotation text floats near the date stamp in teal: 'Still operating?']
VO: A stranger Googles your product. Clean website. Good reviews. They tap your Instagram link. Last post: nine weeks ago.

[SCENE 3 — Side-by-side cut: left panel shows the quiet desaturated grid; right panel shows a competitor's active grid, recent thumbnails in full color, multiple recent posts visible.]
VO: Their thought process takes about thirty seconds. Still operating? Hard to tell. Competitor posted eleven times this month. Going with the other one.

[SCENE 4 — Return to single phone screen. Annotation text appears: 'A quiet feed is a signal.' Slow zoom out to reveal the faint hand holding the phone.]
VO: A quiet feed is a signal. You may not have meant to send it — but they already read it.

[SCENE 5 — Final frame. Fenrik Studio logo appears centered on a clean off-white background. Single line below: 'Keep the signal on.']
VO: [no spoken line — logo hold]

linkedin.caption:
A potential buyer finds your business through a Google search. Website looks credible. Reviews are solid. They click your Instagram link — and the last post is nine weeks old.

In the next thirty seconds, they've moved on to a competitor whose feed has been active all month.

product_role: fenrik Studio is introduced at the resolution point as the practical fix — not a creative tool, not a platform, just a service that keeps the feed moving so the signal stays on. The proof point used is that the first content package is free and requires only a website URL, which removes the barrier that caused the silence in the first place.
narrative_arc: BEFORE: A stranger discovers a brand through a Google search result. Everything looks credible — clean website, decent reviews, professional bio. They tap the Instagram link. The feed loads. Last post: nine weeks ago. CHANGE: The video narrates the stranger's thought process in real time, framed as a series of brief, factual observations — 'Still operating? Hard to tell.' / 'Competitor has posted eleven times this month.' / 'Going with the other one.' No drama. No accusation. Just the logic. AFTER: The brand with the active feed gets the inquiry. The brand with the quiet one does not. The video closes with a single factual statement: a feed that stopped is a signal, whether the business meant to send it or not. Then the CTA frames fenrik Studio as the thing that keeps the signal on.
emotional_tone: Quiet and unsettling — not alarming, just factual. The discomfort comes from recognition, not exaggeration. The stranger is not hostile; they are simply making a reasonable decision with the information available. That neutrality is what makes it land.
audience_insight: Founders and small teams rarely think about what their inactive feed communicates to a stranger — they think about the content they haven't made yet, not the impression the silence is already making. Flipping to the customer's POV makes the cost of inactivity concrete without lecturing.

hook: Nine weeks of silence — what does that say about your business?
scenario: A solo SaaS founder checks their own Instagram profile while reviewing their website analytics and realizes the last post went up the day before a product launch — nine weeks ago. The website looks professional. The social feed looks abandoned. They had not considered that a potential customer would see both in the same session.

video.script:
[SCENE 1 — Phone screen fills frame. Instagram profile grid loads. Thumbnails slightly desaturated. Date stamp visible: '9 weeks ago.']
VO: Nine weeks of silence — what does that say about your business?

[SCENE 2 — Subtle zoom onto the profile bio and grid. Annotation text floats near the date stamp in teal: 'Still operating?']
VO: A stranger Googles your product. Clean website. Good reviews. They tap your Instagram link. Last post: nine weeks ago.

[SCENE 3 — Side-by-side cut: left panel shows the quiet desaturated grid; right panel shows a competitor's active grid, recent thumbnails in full color, multiple recent posts visible.]
VO: Their thought process takes about thirty seconds. Still operating? Hard to tell. Competitor posted eleven times this month. Going with the other one.

[SCENE 4 — Return to single phone screen. Annotation text appears: 'A quiet feed is a signal.' Slow zoom out to reveal the faint hand holding the phone.]
VO: A quiet feed is a signal. You may not have meant to send it — but they already read it.

[SCENE 5 — Final frame. Fenrik Studio logo appears centered on a clean off-white background. Single line below: 'Keep the signal on.']
VO: [no spoken line — logo hold]
video.concept: A micro case told entirely from a stranger's point of view. A potential customer Googles a SaaS tool, finds the Instagram link, taps it — and lands on a feed where the last post is nine weeks old. The video narrates the stranger's thirty-second mental checklist in real time: brief, factual, unhurried. No drama. Just the logic that leads them to choose the competitor instead. The resolution reframes the quiet feed as an unintended signal — and positions fenrik Studio as the practical fix that keeps the signal on.
